opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it less as "DeepMind can't keep people" and more as a structural tension that any big-lab AI for Science effort runs into.

First, there's a mismatch between how science gets done and how a large corporate lab sets priorities. AlphaFold was a perfect case: a well-defined problem, a clean benchmark in CASP, decades of curated data in the PDB, and a result you could validate. Most scientific problems aren't like that. Once you move into materials, chemistry, or biology beyond structure, you need wet labs, experimental feedback loops, and years of iteration. A company whose center of gravity has shifted toward Gemini and general-purpose models will naturally pull compute, talent, and leadership attention toward that core product. Scientists who joined to work on a specific domain problem can start to feel they're a side project.

Second, the market changed underneath them. A few years ago, if you wanted to do frontier AI for Science with serious compute, DeepMind was one of very few places that could support it. Now there's a lot of venture money flowing into AI-for-drug-discovery, materials, and "AI scientist" startups, and investors are very willing to back someone with a DeepMind pedigree. So the outside option got much better: you can own your direction, have real equity upside, and build the experimental infrastructure yourself instead of negotiating for it internally.

Third, credit and ownership. A breakthrough like AlphaFold produces a lot of recognition, but inside a big organization that recognition gets concentrated. For ambitious researchers, the thinking becomes: if I'm going to spend the next ten years on a hard scientific problem, I'd rather it be mine.

And finally, there's a genuine strategic question about whether AI for Science is best done inside a foundation-model company at all. One view is that general models will eventually subsume domain-specific work, so the lab focuses there. The other view is that science needs tight coupling with experiments and domain experts, which favors smaller, focused organizations. People who believe the second view are, almost by definition, the ones most likely to leave.

So I'd read the departures less as a failure of DeepMind specifically and more as a sign that the field is maturing. The idea has been proven, and now it's dispersing into an ecosystem of companies, each trying to own a piece of the scientific stack.

r001.rationale: The response says DeepMind is shifting attention toward Gemini and general-purpose models, but does not connect that shift to making Gemini competitive with leading AI models.

r002.rationale: The response describes company priorities pulling resources toward core products while researchers who joined for specific scientific problems may feel sidelined, capturing the tension with their research aspirations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to start from what DeepMind was built to be. It was founded as a research lab, almost an academic institution with a very large compute budget. The people who joined in those early years came for a specific reason: they wanted to work on fundamental problems, protein folding, weather, materials, fusion control, things where the payoff is scientific understanding rather than a product. AlphaFold was the proof that this model could work.

But the center of gravity has shifted. After the ChatGPT moment, Google essentially merged Brain and DeepMind and pointed the whole organization at Gemini. That is a rational business decision, but it changes the daily reality for a scientist. Suddenly the compute allocation conversations are about frontier model training runs. The reviews are about shipping. The people getting promoted are the ones close to the product. If you are a chemist or a biologist who joined to do science, you feel like a guest in someone else's house.

The second thing is that the outside world now offers a real alternative. Five years ago, if you wanted to do AI for Science at scale, DeepMind was almost the only place. Now there is Isomorphic as a spinout, there are well-funded startups in drug discovery and materials, there are national labs and universities that finally have serious GPU clusters, and venture money is very willing to back a team with a DeepMind pedigree. So the switching cost has collapsed. A scientist can leave, keep working on the same problem, own the direction, and usually make more money.

And the third thing is more cultural. AI for Science has a very different rhythm from frontier model development. A protein or a materials project might take three years and you need patient leadership that accepts a quiet period with no demos. The frontier race runs on quarters, sometimes weeks. When those two rhythms share one organization, the slower one loses the internal competition for attention, even if nobody intends it.

So I don't read the departures as DeepMind failing. I read them as a sign that the field matured. DeepMind trained a generation of people to believe this kind of work is possible, and now those people have places to go. The question for Google is whether it wants to keep a real science lab inside a product company, and be honest about the cost of that, or whether it is comfortable being the place people start and then leave.

r001.rationale: The response says that after the ChatGPT moment Google directed the organization toward Gemini, shifting attention and compute to frontier model training. This communicates the shift toward making Gemini competitive with leading models.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts organizing the group around Gemini and product shipping with scientists’ desire to pursue science on longer timelines and to own their research direction.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty comes from a tension between the time horizon of science and the priorities of a large technology company. AI for Science can require years of work, and progress isn’t always predictable. A company also has to decide how much computing power and talent to put toward research versus products with more immediate returns.

For a scientist, resources matter, but so does the freedom to choose a problem and stay with it. Even a very well-funded lab can struggle to retain people if they feel that their research direction depends on shifting organizational priorities.

And once a field looks promising, researchers have more options. They may want to build their own team, start a company, or return to academia. So I wouldn’t automatically interpret departures as a failure of the research environment. The question is whether people are leaving to pursue opportunities that success has opened up, or because they can no longer do the work they care about. Without knowing the individual circumstances, I’d be cautious about drawing that conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response discusses company priorities and research versus products, but does not attribute a near-term shift to making Gemini competitive with leading AI models.

r002.rationale: It contrasts organizational priorities with researchers’ freedom to choose problems, but does not identify organizing a large team around a dominant project as the specific tension.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame it as a tension between the time horizon of science and the priorities of a large company. AI for Science can take years to produce a result that matters, and even then, the commercial value may be uncertain. Scientists need room to pursue those questions, while a company has to decide where to put its computing resources and talent.

There’s also the question of autonomy. Once researchers see a promising direction, they may want to build their own team and set their own agenda. DeepMind can offer extraordinary resources, but resources aren’t the only thing that keeps a scientist somewhere.

I wouldn’t assume every departure has the same explanation. The broader challenge is whether an organization can give scientists sustained support, freedom, and recognition while its business priorities evolve.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shifting business priorities generally, but does not mention Gemini, making it competitive with leading models, or a near-term shift away from AI for Science.

r002.rationale: It contrasts company priorities with researchers’ desire to set their own agendas, but does not identify organizing a large research team around a dominant project as the tension.
